name: Cadmium Lemon
lede: Cadmium Lemon is a bright greenish yellow sold in artists' tubes; it belongs to the cadmium family first made in 1820.

sections.title: A cadmium yellow
sections.body: Paterson dates cadmium yellow to 1820, made from cadmium sulphide, and says artists used it extensively in the nineteenth century [1]. He lists *cadmium lemon* separately among yellows and defines it as a bright greenish yellow, yet his entry for cadmium yellow says a cadmium lemon yellow has a more orangey hue [1]. The entries pull in different directions, which shows how little a shade name fixes [1][2]. Paterson also notes that cadmium pigments first came into use in the 1820s, with Monet among their fans [1].

sections.title: In the painter's kit
sections.body: A modern color-mixing text by Gurney lists cadmium lemon among the few tube colors for a gamut map: pyrrole red, cadmium yellow, cadmium lemon, ultramarine blue and titanium white [3]. Compare [[cadmium-orange]], [[lemon-yellow]] and [[canary]].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The color shown, #C1B331, is a dull olive-leaning yellow, darker than a tube of cadmium lemon would look [4]. It is the library's average for the name, and screen colors are approximate [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Only 41 of 23,781 archive paintings contain this exact swatch, as photographed [5]. It is a highlight color 95 percent of the time, and it peaks in the 1890s, with Pierre Bonnard using it in 3 of his 45 paintings [5]. Matches are colors, not pigment identifications [5].
